introduction: The English B School-Based Assessment is a portfolio of responses to the literature you have studied. It rewards close reading and independent thinking, so the evidence you select matters more than the length of your writing. The tasks below map the stages of building that portfolio; check the current CSEC syllabus for the exact marks and word limits for your examination session.

tasks.title: Selecting Your Texts
tasks.explanation: Choose the poems, play and prose works you will respond to for the examination you are sitting, and record the exact titles and authors.

tasks.title: Close Reading Notes
tasks.explanation: For each text, note its subject, themes, key techniques and three or four supporting quotations with their sources.

tasks.title: Analytical Response
tasks.explanation: Write a developed response to a question on one text, using point-evidence-explanation and a clear line of argument.

tasks.title: Comparison of Two Texts
tasks.explanation: Compare two texts on a shared basis such as theme, tone or treatment of place, moving between them throughout the response.

tasks.title: Creative Response
tasks.explanation: Respond creatively to a text — a poem in the voice of a character, a diary entry, a missing scene — with a short commentary on your choices.

tasks.title: Presentation and Accuracy
tasks.explanation: Present the portfolio clearly: contents page, accurate quotations with titles, correct spelling of names and titles, and consistent tense.

sampleTitle: How does the poet present the sea as both a threat and a source of life in 'The Sea in September'?

sample.body: This response argues that the poet uses the sea as a metaphor for Caribbean history: beautiful, sustaining and dangerous at the same time.
sample.tips: State your line of argument in one sentence before you begin to write.

sample.body: The poet describes the waves as 'climbing the wall with fists of salt'. The personification of the waves as fighters gives the sea a violent, human will, and the word 'salt' links that violence to sweat and toil on the plantation. The image suggests a sea that has taken lives as well as fed them.
sample.tips: Quote briefly, analyse the exact words, and connect the effect to your argument.

marking: Marks reward accurate knowledge of the texts, analysis of language and technique, a sustained line of argument, relevant evidence and control of written English. Retelling the plot earns little.
checklist: Line of argument stated and sustained
Techniques named and their effects analysed
Comparisons organised around a shared basis

pages.heading: Method: how the texts were chosen, read and written about
pages.body:
Method: how the texts were chosen, read and written about. The portfolio began with the reading list, not with the writing. Each of the four texts was read twice: the first pass simply for what happens, the second with a pencil, marking every place where the language did something the plain sense of the sentence did not. Only after that second pass did I choose a question, and I chose it because 'The Sea in September' gave me two clear opposites to argue about - the sea as the thing that feeds the village and the thing that empties it.

The notes were then built in a fixed order so that the evidence came before the argument. For each text I made a table with three columns: the technique, the exact words the poet used, and the effect those words create. Keeping the quotation in the middle column was the discipline that mattered most, because it stopped me drifting into retelling. A quotation was only allowed into an essay if I could say what it did in the sentence, not merely what it said. Each response was drafted long, cut by about a fifth, and then read aloud once to catch tense slips.
bullets: Read each text twice: once for sense, once for language
Build a three-column note table before choosing a question
Draft long, cut by about a fifth, then read aloud for tense

pages.heading: Choice of Texts: the texts studied and why each was kept
pages.body: Choice of Texts: the four texts and the reason each was kept. The four texts below were read in full before any response was written. Each was kept for a different reason, and each reason is recorded here so that the portfolio shows deliberate selection rather than a list of whatever was nearest to hand. Every title, author, candidate and school named in this worked example is invented; the selection logic is the part being demonstrated. The two poems were paired early because they treat the same island weather from opposite moods: one solemn, one comic. The play was kept for the creative response, where a minor character's voice could be borrowed, and the prose extract was kept because its imagery of labour gave the comparison a third register to test against.

pages.heading: Close Reading of 'The Sea in September': technique, quotation and effect
pages.body: The table below is the note sheet for the main text, kept in the form the portfolio uses: the technique, the exact words, and the effect. Two rows concern the same phrase doing two jobs, because that overlap is the evidence the analytical response depends on. Quotations are held to a phrase so that the words can be held in mind while the effect is explained.

table.caption: Close reading notes: 'The Sea in September' (all lines invented for this sample)
rows: Personification
the waves are 'climbing the wall with fists of salt'
gives the sea a fighter's will, so its power feels deliberate and personal.
Metaphor
'the sea keeps two ledgers: one of what it took, one of what it gave'
turns the sea into a record-keeper, hinting at the island's debt to the water.
Imagery (sight and sound)
'September writes its name in the sand and the tide rubs it out'
makes the month a signature that is washed away - beauty and loss in one image.
Repetition
'again, again, again' at the end of three stanzas
mimics the returning tide, and the returning fear of the fishing families.
Tone
the quiet line 'and still the boats go out'
the calm understatement makes the courage of the fishermen feel ordinary and daily.

pages.heading: Close Reading of 'Market Day, Half-Way-Tree': technique, quotation and effect
pages.body: The second note sheet covers the comparison text. Its purpose is to record what this poem does differently from the first, so that a pattern can be seen before any comparison is written: where the sea poem reaches for ledger and signature, the market poem reaches for a hush, a haggling scale and one small bird. Recording the effects separately first stopped the comparison from becoming a list of similarities.

table.caption: Close reading notes: 'Market Day, Half-Way-Tree' (all lines invented for this sample)
rows: Sound
'the awnings breathe once, then hold their breath'
half-rhyme and hush imitate the pause in trade just before the heat breaks.
Simile
'a scale that argues with the sun'
the market's bargaining is set against the sun as an equal opponent.
Diction (dialect)
'the price is the price, my girl'
the flat repetition of a vendor's phrase carries the whole bargaining culture.
Contrast
the roar of the crowd against 'one bird doing sums in the eaves'
the small, precise sound makes the crowd's noise feel temporary next to nature.

pages.heading: Results: the analytical response as submitted (First Response)
pages.body:
Response as submitted. The poem presents the sea as a provider and a threat at the same time, and it does this by using one set of images for both jobs. The clearest example opens the second stanza, where the waves are 'climbing the wall with fists of salt'. The personification gives the water a fighter's body and a fighter's intention: it is not weather, it is an opponent choosing to come over. The word 'salt' does the second job in the same phrase, because salt is what preserves the catch the village lives on and what ruins the ground it grows food in. A threat and a livelihood are made of the same material, so the reader cannot separate them.

The ledger metaphor extends this. When the poem says the sea 'keeps two ledgers: one of what it took, one of what it gave', it turns the water into an accountant, and the accounting is deliberately even. The image also links the sea to the island's history of accounts kept elsewhere, so the poem's private grief about drowned fishermen carries a public weight. That double meaning is what lifts the stanza above a description of rough weather.

Structure supports the argument. The repeated 'again, again, again' at the close of three stanzas mimics the returning tide, and the return is the point: the village is not rescued once, it is spared repeatedly, and each sparing is temporary. Against that repetition the poet places one quiet line - 'and still the boats go out'. The calm understatement, after all the noise of the waves, presents courage as an ordinary daily habit rather than a dramatic choice. The final image, 'September writes its name in the sand and the tide rubs it out', closes the argument where it began: the same water that erases the month is the water that keeps the month's people fed.

The evidence therefore answers the question with a qualified yes. The sea is presented as both threat and source of life, but not in alternation - the poem fuses the two, which is why its ending feels neither resigned nor grateful. If it separated them, the poem would take a side; by holding them in one image it forces the reader to hold both.
bullets: Question: How does the poet present the sea as both a threat and a source of life in 'The Sea in September'?

Statement of focus: this response argues that the poet never separates the two faces of the sea. The threat and the living are carried by the same images, so that the village's food and the village's danger arrive in the same line of verse - which is why the poem refuses to end in either fear or gratitude.
Four paragraphs: fusion of threat and life, the ledger metaphor, structure, qualified conclusion

pages.heading: Results: the comparative response as submitted
pages.body:
Comparative response: two poems on one town, two different kinds of heat. This response compares 'The Sea in September' with 'Market Day, Half-Way-Tree' on the basis of tone, and argues that the difference between the two poems is a difference in what the poets are willing to let nature do. Both poems place an ordinary community beside an enormous natural force; the first poem respects that force, the second teases it.

Where Marchand elevates, Balfour deflates. Marchand's waves 'climb' a wall with 'fists of salt', which gives the sea intention and menace; Balfour's heat is comic and domestic, as in 'the awnings breathe once, then hold their breath'. Both poems personify, but the effect is opposite in direction: one makes the natural world a fighter, the other makes it a tired shopper. The verb choice carries the whole difference. 'Climbing' is effort and threat; 'breathe' is ordinary and slightly absurd, and the market, not the sky, is what fills with life.

The second basis of comparison is scale. Marchand keeps the human figures small against the water: the boats go out, unnamed, into a sea that keeps records. Balfour brings the human noise forward and makes the natural detail small and precise instead, as when 'one bird doing sums in the eaves' is set against the roar of the crowd. The two poets therefore reverse the same proportion. What is large in one poem is domestic in the other, and the reader's sympathy is directed accordingly - outward to a community's survival in the first, inward to a single bargaining voice in the second.

The comparison matters because it shows that tone is not decoration but a way of arguing. Reading the poems together, the heat of the market square makes the sea poem's solemnity feel chosen rather than automatic: Marchand could have written the same scene as comedy and did not. Where Balfour's diction lets a vendor's flat 'the price is the price, my girl' stand as the wisdom of the poem, Marchand's diction reaches for the ledger and the signature. Same island, same weather, opposite verdicts - which is exactly why comparing them proves that each poet is doing something deliberate with the language rather than simply describing what everyone can see.
bullets: Basis of comparison: tone, held across every paragraph
Each paragraph moves between the two poems rather than alternating blocks
Verdict: same island, same weather, opposite conclusions - so the solemnity is a choice

pages.heading: Creative or Personal Response: a poem in the voice of the sister, with commentary
pages.body:
Creative response: a poem in the voice of the fisherman's wife, with commentary. In 'The River Between Us' the sister who stays behind has four lines in the whole play, and those four lines are all worry. This response gives her the poem she does not get in the script. It is written in her voice, in plain short lines, because the play's own language for her is plain and short.

The Chosen Side

My brother keeps the far bank.
I keep the kettle, the lamp, the ledger of what the water owes.
He says the river is a road.
I say a road does not take the bridge with it.
When the rain comes I count the spaces where the boats were,
and I hang his shirt on the line anyway,
so the wind can do the arguing for me.

Commentary on the choices. The form is a short free-verse poem rather than a diary entry because the sister's character is defined by what she does not say, and a diary would have forced her to explain herself. The title 'The Chosen Side' is ironic: nobody in the play chooses a bank, the river does the choosing, and the phrase lets the poem borrow the play's central idea without repeating its dialogue. The kettle, lamp and shirt are taken from the play's stage directions rather than invented, so the poem stays anchored in the world of the script. The repetition of counting - 'I count the spaces where the boats were' - echoes the play's own habit of counting things, and it lets the wife's grief appear as housekeeping, which is how the play shows it. The final image hands the argument to the wind, which keeps the poem's last word passive in the same way the sister is, and avoids the temptation to give her a speech the playwright never wrote.
bullets: Form chosen: short free verse, because the character is defined by what she does not say
Props borrowed from the play's stage directions so the poem stays in the script's world
Commentary explains title, repetition and the passive ending

pages.heading: Discussion: what the close reading and the comparison showed
pages.body:
Discussion: what the close reading and the comparison showed. Two things became clear while the portfolio was being built, and both of them changed how the later responses were written. The first is that a technique is only worth naming if the effect can be stated in the same sentence. The close-reading tables forced this, because the third column had to be a consequence and not a label: 'the awnings breathe' is only useful evidence once the hush before the heat breaks has been described as its effect. Naming the technique without the effect produced empty sentences, and those sentences were the first thing cut from every draft.

The second finding is that comparison is stronger when it is organised around a single basis. Comparing the poems through tone meant that every paragraph could return to the same question: what is each poet willing to let nature do? When the first draft of the comparative response tried to cover tone, theme and structure at once, the paragraphs became separate mini-essays and the argument disappeared. Restricting the comparison to tone, and then showing that tone is a form of argument, produced a response that moved between the two texts in every paragraph rather than alternating blocks of summary.

A third, smaller lesson concerns quotation length. The shortest quotations did the most work, because a phrase like 'the price is the price, my girl' can be held in the reader's mind while its effect is explained, whereas a long quoted sentence has to be re-read before it can be analysed. This is why the final drafts quote in phrase rather than in sentence, and why every quotation in the portfolio is followed by analysis of specific words rather than a general comment on the passage.
bullets: A technique is only evidence once its effect is stated in the same sentence
Comparison needs one basis, or the paragraphs become separate mini-essays
Short quotations carry more analytical weight than long ones

pages.heading: Conclusion: what the portfolio demonstrates, and what would change
pages.body:
Conclusion: what the portfolio demonstrates and what would change next time. The portfolio answers the question it set itself. In 'The Sea in September' the sea is presented as a threat and as a source of life through the same images rather than through separate ones, and the poem's structure - repetition of the returning tide, closed by one quiet line - makes that fusion the argument rather than the background. Comparing the poem with 'Market Day, Half-Way-Tree' showed that this solemnity is a choice: the same weather can be written as comedy, and the difference lies in verbs, diction and scale.

Three things would be done differently. First, the notes for the prose extract would be made before the comparison was planned, because reading the extract last meant that a third register of imagery arrived too late to be used in the comparative response. Second, the creative response would be drafted earlier, while the play was still fresh, instead of after the analytical essay had fixed a more formal voice in my head. Third, the portfolio would be assembled in a folder from the first week, so that the contents page was maintained rather than reconstructed at the end. Each of these is a matter of order rather than of effort, and order is what the portfolio finally demonstrates: evidence gathered before argument, quotation before comment, and one clear question carried all the way to the end.
bullets: The sea is threat and life through the same images, not through alternating ones
The comparison proves the solemn tone is deliberate rather than automatic
Three changes next time: notes for the prose earlier, the creative piece earlier, a folder from week one

pages.heading: Presentation and accuracy: the final check before submission
pages.body: Presentation and accuracy: the final check before submission. The portfolio was checked against the requirements one at a time, and the table below records how each was met. Titles and authors were copied from the contents page onto every response so that a reader moving between parts never has to guess which text is being discussed. Quotations were checked against the notes, and every one was shortened to a phrase wherever the longer form added nothing. Spellings of names and titles were verified letter by letter, and tense was kept consistent by reading each response aloud once. The contents page lists the six parts in the order they are submitted, with the marks our guide gives each part, so an examiner can see at a glance that nothing is missing.

pages.heading: Sources and honesty note for this worked example
pages.body: Every text named in this portfolio - 'The Sea in September', 'Market Day, Half-Way-Tree', 'The River Between Us' and 'Salt and Cane' - and every author named with them, every quotation, the candidate, the centre and the teacher are invented for this sample. No line of any real poem, play, novel, story or other published work is reproduced here, and no examination board's exemplar material has been used. The purpose of the sample is to show the shape of a strong portfolio: texts chosen deliberately, evidence recorded before argument, every quotation explained at the level of the word, a comparison organised on one basis, and a presentation check carried out before submission. Study the shape, then build your own portfolio around the texts you are actually studying, because the marks are earned by your own reading of your own texts.
bullets: All texts, authors and quotations invented - nothing reproduced from any published work
Original worked example written for CSEC Compass, not a real candidate's submission
Use it as a model of method; the analysis must be your own

examinerNotes: Every claim about a technique is paired with the exact words that carry it, so the analysis never drifts into retelling - the single thing that separates a strong English B response from a summary.
The comparison is built on one basis and held across every paragraph, which is what makes it a comparison rather than two short essays placed next to each other.

The creative response is a genuine response to the text rather than a free piece: the props come from the play's stage directions, the title borrows its central idea, and the commentary justifies form, repetition and the passive ending.

Presentation marks are earned by a real contents page, accurate titles and authors, consistent short quotation and a tense read-through - the parts of a portfolio that candidates most often leave to the last evening.
